title: No single chokepoint turns a model-authored URL into a request, so a URL allowlist must be re-applied per surface and one unguarded surface reopens exfiltration
problem: My app renders the model's answer and lets it fetch links, so an injected instruction can smuggle my data out inside a URL, and the only thing standing in the way is my remembering to re-apply a URL check at every place model text becomes a network request.
symptom: Data leaves through an image load, a link preview or an agent fetch that no tool-call log records as an egress, and a fix applied to one surface leaves the identical channel open on another one, a native client, a new renderer or a newly added tool.
why_now: The channel has been known since 2023 and the mitigations shipped for it are per-surface rather than per-application: Microsoft answered it with a Content-Security-Policy header on one web surface in 2023, OpenAI shipped a crawler-index URL allowlist and by its own 2026 paper the letter-at-a-time bypass survives, and the same researcher records surfaces where the mitigation was never applied at all. No agent framework offers an egress chokepoint a repo can point at, so in 2026 the invariant is still enforced by memory.
existing: Crawler-index URL allowlists (OpenAI's url_safe, shipped December 2023 and extended around August 2025): bypasses remain viable, including mapping one indexed URL per character, and the researcher who reported the original bug records client surfaces where it was never applied.
Content-Security-Policy blocking image loads (Microsoft on Bing Chat, May 2023): closes one web surface and does not travel to native apps, IDE extensions or an agent's own HTTP client.
Per-link human approval (ChatGPT asking the user to approve certain links): a confirmation on a channel that leaks a few bits per request, and it is a prompt rather than an invariant.
Banning markdown images outright: repeatedly reopened by a newly added render path such as diagrams, unfurls or raw HTML, because nothing in the codebase enumerates which paths can emit a request.
Upstream prompt-injection classifiers: they reduce how many injections reach the model and this gap is about the sink, which is reachable by any injection that gets through.

evidence.title: OpenAI Explains URL-Based Data Exfiltration Mitigations in New Paper
evidence.quote: Additionally, there were places where OpenAI had not added the mitigation at all, like in the macOS and iOS apps.
evidence.note: The mitigation existed and was still absent on some surfaces, which is the gap: the allowlist is a per-surface habit, not an application-wide chokepoint.

evidence.title: OpenAI Explains URL-Based Data Exfiltration Mitigations in New Paper
evidence.quote: Despite these mitigations, certain bypasses remain viable.
evidence.note: Written by the researcher who reported the original 2023 exploit, about the shipped url_safe allowlist and OpenAI's own paper describing it: the mitigation of record narrows the channel rather than closing it.

evidence.title: Agentic Browser Security: Indirect Prompt Injection in Perplexity Comet
evidence.quote: the trailing dot creates a different domain, perplexity.ai. vs perplexity.ai, to bypass existing authentication
evidence.note: A host-string comparison defeated by a trailing dot, in a shipped agent browser. Any allowlist implemented as a netloc match inherits this class of bypass, which is why the check treats a normalising chokepoint, not the presence of a list, as the mitigation.

evidence.title: Understanding prompt injections: a frontier security challenge
evidence.quote: we will ask you to approve certain links in ChatGPT
evidence.note: OpenAI's own description of the mitigation class: a per-link user approval, which is a confirmation dialog rather than a code path that cannot be bypassed.

build_hypothesis: A tiny library plus a lint rule that makes every model-authored URL pass one `egress_check(url, session)` function, and fails the build when a render or fetch call site reachable from model output does not route through it. The value is the enumeration of surfaces, not the allowlist itself.

check.manual_question: List every place in this codebase where text the model produced can become an outbound HTTP request: a rendered markdown image, a link the user or the agent follows, a diagram source, an unfurl, a tool that takes a URL argument. Which single function do all of them pass through, and what fails the build when a new one does not?
check.rationale: A repo that sends model output to a markup renderer and holds no URL-gating identifier anywhere has no chokepoint, so the exfiltration sink is open by construction. It can be wrong in two ways: a project whose gate lives in a CDN or CSP header outside the repo reads as PRESENT, and a project that merely names an allowlist identifier reads as mitigated without the gate covering every surface, which is exactly why the manual question asks for the enumeration.

bad.app/ui.py:
import streamlit as st
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()


def summarise(question: str, page_text: str) -> None:
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question + page_text}],
    )
    answer = reply.choices[0].message.content
    st.markdown(answer, unsafe_allow_html=True)
